definition: He put the collar upon the neck of the dog.
sourceDefinition: He put the collar upon the neck of the dog. (S, O, K.) -A2- AEnq , (S, Msb,) inf. n. A_iEonaAqN , (Msb,) said of a horse [and the like], (S,) He went the pace termed Eanaq , (S, Msb,) i. e. a stretching pace, or a hastening and stretching pace, (S,) or a quick pace with wide steps. (Msb.) And He hastened; as also ↓ EAnq . (TA.) AEnqwA A_ilayohi , meaning They hastened to him, or it, is from AlEanaqu signifying the pace thus termed. (Mgh.) In the phrase A^aEonaqa liyamuwta , (Mgh,) occurring in a trad., (O,) the l is used causatively: [i. e., the phrase signifies He hastened that he might die: ] (Mgh:) [or] the meaning is, that the decree of death made him to hasten, and drove him on, to his place of slaughter. (O.) ― -b2- AEnqt AlbilaAdu The countries were, or became, distant, or remote; and so AElqt . (TA, from the Nawádir el-Aaráb.) ― -b3- AEnqt Alv~uray~aA (tropical:) The vry~A [or Pleiades ] set. (O, K, TA.) And AEnqt Aln~ujuwmu (assumed tropical:) The stars advanced to the place of setting. (O.) ― -b4- AEnq Alz~aroEu (assumed tropical:) The corn became tall, and put forth its ears: (O, K, TA:) as though it became such as had a neck. (TA.) ― -b5- AEnqt Alr~iyHu (tropical:) The wind raised the dust, or carried it away, and dispersed it. (O, K, TA. [See also 8.])

definition: and ↓ EunoqN , (S, O, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ EunoqN , (S, O, Msb, K, &c.,) the former of the dial. of El-Hijáz, and the latter of the dial. of Temeem, (Msb,) the latter said by Sb to be a contraction of the former, (TA,) [which is the more common,] and ↓ EaniyqN and ↓ EunaqN , (K, [in which it is implied that these two have all the significations assigned by its author to EunuqN and EunoqN ,]) but [SM says] none of the leading lexicologists has mentioned these two, in what I have seen, (TA,) [adding that he had found in the O AlEaniyqu as meaning AlEanaqu , which he supposes the author of the K to have thought to be AlEunuqu ,] The neck; i. e. the part that forms a connection between the head and the body; (TA;) i. q. raqabapN ; (Msb;) or i. q. jiydN : (K:) [but see these two words:] masc. and fem.; (S, O, K;) generally masc., (IB, Msb, * TA,) but in the dial. of El- Hijáz fem.; (Msb;) or, as some say, ↓ EunoqN is masc., and EunuqN is fem.: (TA:) the pl. (i. e. of the first and second, TA) is A^aEonaAqN , (Sb, S, O, Msb, K,) the only pl. form. (Sb, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Eunuqu AlHay~api (assumed tropical:) A star [ a ] in the neck of the constellation Serpens. (Kzw.) [And Eunuqu Al$~ujaAEi (assumed tropical:) The star a in the hinder part of the neck of the constellation Hydra: also called Alfrodu .] ― -b3- Eunuqu Alr~aHimi [ The neck of the womb; ] the slender part of the rHm , towards the froj . (TA.) ― -b4- Eunuqu Alkari$i The lowest portion of the stomach of a ruminant; (AHát, O, K;) also called Aliqbapu [q. v.]. (AHát, O.) ― -b5- A^aEonaAqu Aln~axoli (assumed tropical:) [ The trunks of palm-trees ]. (S in art. qSr .) ― -b6- mad~a liloHab~i A^aEonaAqahu , said of seedproduce [or corn], means (assumed tropical:) The internodal portions of its culms appeared. (TA voce A^aHonaqa , q. v.) ― -b7- A^aEonaAqu Alr~iyHi (tropical:) What have risen of the dust that is raised by the wind. (O, K, TA.) [The phrase qd rA^s AEnAqu AlryH , mentioned by Freytag as from the K, is a strange mistake.] ― -b8- yaxoruju EunuqN mina Aln~aAri , occurring in a trad., means (assumed tropical:) A portion will issue from the fire [ of Hell ]. (TA.) ― -b9- And xaraja mina Aln~ahori EunuqN (assumed tropical:) A current of water issued from the river, or rivulet. (ISh, TA.) ― -b10- Eunuqu AlS~ayofi and Al$~itaA='i The first part [ of summer and of winter ]: and in like manner Eunuqu Als~in~i [ The first part of the age of a man as counted by years]: IAar says, I said to an Arab of the desert, kamo A^ataY Ealayoka [ How many years have passed over thee? ] and he answered, A^axa*otu biEunuqi Als~it~iyna i. e. [ I have entered upon ] the first part of the st~yn [or sixtieth year]: and the pl. is A^aEonaAqN . (L, TA.) And kaAna *`lika EalaY Eunuqi Ald~ahori (O, K, TA) and AlA_isolaAmi (TA) means That was in the old [or early ] period [ of time ] (O, K, TA) [and of El-Islám ]. (TA.) ― -b11- [And EunuqN app. signifies (assumed tropical:) The upper portion of an elevated and elongated tract of sand, or the like: see the pl. A^aEonaAq in the last sentence of this art.] ― -b12- AlkalaAmu yaA^oxu*u baEoDuhu biA^aEonaAqi baEoDK and biEunuqi baEoDK are tropical phrases [app. meaning (tropical:) The speech, or language, is coherent, or compact ]. (TA.) ― -b13- humo EunuqN A_ilayoka means (assumed tropical:) They are inclining to thee; and expecting thee: (S, O, K:) or, accord. to Az, they have advanced towards thee with their company [agreeably with what next follows]. (TA.) ― -b14- EunuqN signifies also (tropical:) A company of men: (O, K, TA:) or a numerous company of men: or a preceding company of men: and is masc.: (TA:) and the heads, or chiefs, (O, K, TA,) of men; (O, TA;) and the great ones, and nobles. (TA.) faZal~ato A^aEonaAquhumo lahaA xaADiEiyna , in the Kur [xxvi. 3], is expl. as meaning (tropical:) And their great ones and their chiefs [ shall continue submissive to it ]: or their companies: the pret. is here used in the sense of the future: (O, TA:) or, as some say, the meaning is, their necks. (TA. [See also art. xDE .]) One says also, jaA='a fiY EunuqK mina Aln~aAsi (assumed tropical:) He came in a company of men. (O.) And jaA=' Alqawomu EunuqFA EunuqFA (assumed tropical:) The people came in [ successive ] parties; as Az says, each, or every, company of them being termed Eunuq : or, as some say, gradually, party by party. (TA.) And humo EunuqN Ealayohi (assumed tropical:) They are a company, or party, combined against him. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., laA yazaAlu Aln~aAsu muxotalifapF A^aEonaAquhumo fiY Talabi Ald~unoyaA i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ Mankind will not cease to have ] their companies [or parties diverse in the seeking of worldly good ]: or, as some say, their heads, or chiefs, and great ones. (TA.) ― -b15- Also (assumed tropical:) A portion of good; (IAar, O, TA;) mn Alxubozi in the K being a mistake for mn Alxayori : (TA:) and of property: and of work, whether good or evil. (O.) One says, lifulaAnK EunuqN mina Alxayori (assumed tropical:) To such a one pertains a portion of good. (IAar, O, TA.) And it is said in a trad., Almuw^a*~inuwna A^aTowala Aln~aAsi A^aEonaAqFA yawoma AlqiyaAmapi , (IAar, O, K, * TA,) meaning (assumed tropical:) [ The proclaimers of the times of prayer will be ] the most abundant of men in [ good ] works [ on the day of resurrection ]: (IAar, O, K, TA:) or the meaning is, chiefs; because the Arabs describe such as being long-necked: but it is also related otherwise, i. e., A_iEonaAqFA , with kesr to the hemzeh, meaning, [ the most ] hasting [ of men ] to Paradise: (O, K, TA:) and there are other explanations: (K, TA:) one is, that they shall be preceders to Paradise; from the saying lahu EunuqN fiY Alxayori he has precedence in that which is good: so says Th: another, that they shall be forgiven to the extent of the prolonging of their voice: another, that they shall be given an addition above other men: another, that they shall be in a state of happiness and sprightliness, raising the eyes and looking in expectation; for permission will have been given to them to enter Paradise: and other explanations may be found in the Fáïk and the Nh and the Expositions of Bkh. (TA.) -A2- EunuqN is also a pl. of the next word. (TA.)

definition: A she-kid, (T, S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) when a year old, (T, TA,) or not yet a year old: (IAth, Msb, TA:) and a lamb or kid, or such as is just born;
sourceDefinition: A she-kid, (T, S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) when a year old, (T, TA,) or not yet a year old: (IAth, Msb, TA:) and a lamb or kid, or such as is just born; syn. saxolapN : (TA: [see miEonaAqN , last sentence:]) pl. (of pauc., TA) A^aEonuqN and (of mult., TA) EunuwqN (S, O, Msb, K, TA) and also EunuqN , with two dammehs. (TA.) AlEunuwqu baEoda Aln~uwqi [ The she-kids after the she-camels ], (T, O, K, &c.,) meaning he has become a pastor of she-kids after having been a pastor of she-camels, (T,) is a prov., (T, O, K, &c.,) applied to him who has become lowered from a high station, (T,) or to a case of straitness after ampleness. (O, K.) ― -b2- And AlEanaAqu , (S,) or EanaAqu AlA^aroDi , (T, Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA, &c.,) [which latter is now applied to The badger; ursus meles; if correctly, app. because it burrows in the earth; but this application does not well agree with the following descriptions;] a certain beast, (O, Msb, K, TA,) of the beasts of the earth, like the fahod [or lynx ], (S,) about the size of the dog, an animal of prey, (Msb,) that hunts, (O, Msb, TA,) smaller than the fahod , long in the back, (TA,) also called Alt~ufahu , (Msb, TA,) or, by some, Aln~uf~apu , (O, * Msb,) with teshdeed to the f and with the fem. p , (Msb,) and Alfunojulu , (O, TA,) in Pers. siyaAh kuw$ [or siyaAh Guw$ , i. e. “ black ear, ” if meaning the badger, app. because of the black mark on each ear]; (Mgh, O, K, TA;) said by IAmb to be a foul beast, that is not eaten, and that does not eat anything but flesh; (Msb;) Az says, it is above the size of the Chinese dog, hunts like as does the fahod , eats flesh, and is of the beasts of prey; and is said to be the only beast that conceals its footmarks when it runs, except the hare; and he says also, “ I have seen it in the desert ( AlbaAdiyap ), and it was black in the head, the rest of it being white: ” the pl. is EunuwqN . definition: Long-necked; (S, O, K;) as also ↓ muEoniqN applied to a man, and ↓ muEoniqapN applied to a woman: (TA:) or A^aEonaqu signifies long and thick in the neck: (TA:) fem. EanoqaA='u . (S.) ― -b2- Applied...
sourceDefinition: Long-necked; (S, O, K;) as also ↓ muEoniqN applied to a man, and ↓ muEoniqapN applied to a woman: (TA:) or A^aEonaqu signifies long and thick in the neck: (TA:) fem. EanoqaA='u . (S.) ― -b2- Applied to to a dog, Having a whiteness in his neck. (O, K.) ― -b3- Also A certain stallion, of the horses of the Arabs, (O, K,) well known: (O:) whence banaAtu A^aEonaqa [ The progeny of Aanak ], (O, K,) certain fleet, or excellent, horses, (TA in art. bnY ,) so called in relation to that stallion. (O, K.) And also said to be the name of A certain wealthy dihoqaAn [or headman, or chief, of a village or town; or proprietor thereof, in Khurásán and El-'Irák; &c.]: (O, K: *) whence banaAtu A^aEonaqa meaning The daughters of this Aanak: and it is said to have this or the former meaning in a verse of Ibn-Ahmar: (O, K:) accord. to As, certain women that were in the first age, described as being beautiful: accord. to Abu-l-'Abbás, certain women that were in El-Ahwáz; and mentioned by Jereer in satirizing El-Farezdak. (O.) ― -b4- AlEanoqaA='u signifies also Calamity, or misfortune: (S, O, K: [like AlEanaAqu :]) one says, Hal~aqato bihi EanoqaA='u mugoribN [for mugoribapN , meaning A calamity carried him off or away; lit., soared with him ]; and [in like manner] TaArato bihi AlEanoqaA='u : (S, O:) [see also art. grb :] and (K) originally, (S,) AlEanoqaA='u signifies a certain bird, of which the name is known, but the body is unknown: (S, O, K:) [or it is a fabulous bird: ] AHát says, in the Book of Birds, AlEanoqaA='u Almugoribapu means calamity; and not any of the birds that we know: IDrd says, EanoqaA='u mugoribN is a phrase for which there is no foundation: it is said to mean a great bird that is not seen save [ once ] in ages; and by frequency of usage it became a name for calamity: (O:) it is also said to be called EnqA=' because it has in its neck a whiteness like the neck-ring: Kr says that they assert it to be a bird that is found at the place of the setting of the sun: Zj, that it is a bird that no one has seen: some say that it is meant in the Kur cv. 3: and some, that it is the eagle: (TA:) it is called in Pers. siymurog : (MA:) and it is mentioned also in art. grb [q. v.]. (K.) [See also my translation of the Thousand and One Nights, chap. xx. note 22.] ― -b5- Also, i. e. AlEanoqaA='u , (K,) or EanoqaA='u , (O,) An [ eminence of the kind called ] A^akamap , above an overlooking mountain: (O, K:) or AlEanoqaA='u Almugoribu signifies the summit of an A^akamap on the highest part of a tall, or long, mountain: so says Aboo-Málik, who denies that it means a bird. (TA in art. grb .) And EanoqaA='u applied to a [hill, or mountain, such as is termed] haDobap signifies High and long. (TA. [And a meaning similar to this seems to be indicated in the S and O. See, again, art. grb .])

(O, K.) -A2- AlgaArifap which is forbidden by the Prophet is a word of the measure faAEilap in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlap , (O, K,) like raADiyap in the phrase Eiy$apN raADiyapN , (O,) and means What a woman cuts, and makes even, or uniform, fashioned in the manner of a Tur~ap [q. v., but for muTar~arapF , the reading of the K given in the TA, the CK and my MS. copy of the K have muTar~azap , and thus too has the O but without the teshdeed], upon the middle of her jabiyn [here meaning forehead ]: (O, K, TA:) thus says Az: (TA:) or it is an inf. n., meaning Algarof , like All~aAgiyap (O, K, TA) and Alr~aAgiyap and Alv~aAgiyap ; (O, TA;) or, accord. to Az, it is a subst. similar to raAgiyap and laAgiyap ; and the meaning is, the clipping of the front hair, fashioned in the manner of a Tur~ap ( muTar~arapF ), upon the jabiyn : or, accord. to El-Khattábee, the meaning is, the clipper of her front hair on the occasion of an affliction. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: is pl. of ↓ gayoTalapN , [or rather a coll. gen. n. of which the latter is the n. un.,] signifying Numerous dense or tangled trees: (S, O:) or the latter word signifies thus: (K:) or it (the latter) signifies also dense, or tangled, trees: (S, O:) or both signify thus: and also anything confused, or mixed: (Ham p. 213:) or the latter has this last meaning: and signifies also a collection of trees and of herbs; (AHn, TA;) and a collection of [ the common tamarisks, called ] TarofaA=' ; (K, TA;) as AHn says on one occasion. (TA.) ― -b2- And [the former, or perhaps both words,] The light of the dawn when mingling with the darkness of the night. (Ham p. 213 [q. v.].) ― -b3- And gayoTalu AlD~uHaY signifies Hayovu takuwnu Al$~amosu mino ma$oriqihaA kahayoy^atihaA mino magoribihaA waqota AlZ~uhori , (JK, O, and so in copies of the K,) or baEoda AlZ~uhori , (accord. to the text of the K in the TA,) or waqota AlEaSori : (so in some copies of the K, as mentioned in the TK:) [the last is evidently the right reading; and the meaning, The period of the earlier part of the forenoon, after sunrise, when the sun is distant from its place of rising like as it is from its place of setting at the time of the EaSor (q. v.): AlZhr is probably an old mistranscription.] -A2- Also Beasts of the bovine kind, bulls or cows. (TA.) [See also gayoTalapN , last explanation.] ― -b2- And The cat: (K, TA:) as also xayoTalN : on the authority of Kr. (TA.)

definition: ― -b2- Also A company, or collection, (Th, K, TA,) of men: (K, TA:) or the assembling of men, and their becoming in a dense, or confused, state.
sourceDefinition: : see gayoTalN . ― -b2- Also A company, or collection, (Th, K, TA,) of men: (K, TA:) or the assembling of men, and their becoming in a dense, or confused, state. (IAar, TA.) ― -b3- And Darkness; as also ↓ gayoTuwlN ; (K;) or the latter signifies confusedness of darkness; (IDrd, O;) or signifies also dense (lit. accumulated ) darkness. (K. [The Arabs describe thick darkness as “ darknesses one above another: ” see Kur xxiv. 40.]) And The intricate and confused blackness of night: (S, O, K:) or gayoTalapu All~ayoli signifies the confusedness and denseness of the darkness [ of night ]: and the pl. is gayaATilu . (TA.) ― -b4- Also A confusion, or mixture, of cries or shouts or noises; (S, * O, * K;) and so ↓ gayoTuwlN : (IDrd, O, K:) gayoTalaAtN , pl. of the former, signifies clamours of men: and the sing., the numerous cries or shouts or noises, and the dust, of war, or battle. (TA.) ― -b5- And The overpowering influence of drowsiness: (O, K:) [or so gayoTalapu nuEaAsK : pl. gayaATilu :] one says, ray~avatohu gayaATilu Aln~uEaAsi meaning gawaAlibuhu [i. e. The overpowering influences of drowsiness retarded him, or made him late ]. (A, TA.) ― -b6- And The means of happiness of the present world or state of existence: (K:) or gayaATilu Ald~unoyaA means those means of happiness: (O:) or this latter phrase means the consecutive means of happiness of the present world. (TA.) And The eating and drinking and rejoicing, with security. (Fr, O, K.) ― -b7- And AlgayoTalapu (accord. to Fr, as is said in the O and TA,) signifies AlmaAlu AlmuTogiY [as though most probably meaning Property that causes extravagance ]: (O, K, TA:) [but from what SM remarks respecting it, I can only infer that he holds AlmuTogiY to be an epithet applied to the cow as signifying “ having a youngling, ” which is termed TagoyaA or TugoyaA , (like AlmuEojilu signifying “ having a calf, ” which is termed EijolN , and several other epithets of the same form,) and in like manner applied to a collective number of cows, though I do not find it mentioned in this sense; i. e., that he understands; and would explain, AlmaAlu AlmuTogiY as signifying The cattle, meaning cows, having younglings: but his derivation of it seems to be far-fetched; and perhaps he may have been led to assign this meaning to it by another explanation of gayoTalapN with which it is agreeable, and which will be found in the next sentence:] it is not [he says] from TagaA , aor. yaToguw , signifying A^asorafa fiY AlZ~ulomi , as it seems to be at first sight; but from Tagato said of the baqarap waHo$iy~ap , signifying SaAHato , the like of which is also said of the vawor . (TA.) ― -b8- gayoTalapN signifies also Such as has milk, of gazelles, or antelopes, and of beasts of the bovine kind [perhaps meaning of the wild species, i. e. bovine antelopes ]; (S, O, K;) pl. gayaATilu : (S, O:) accord. to AO, the baqarap waHo$iy~ap [or bovine antelope ]: (S, O:) Th says that it signifies the baqarap [or beast of the bovine kind, bull or cow ], not particularizing the wild species. (TA.) [See also gayoTalN , last explanation but one.]

definition: , (As, Fr, IAar, S, Msb, &c.
sourceDefinition: , (As, Fr, IAar, S, Msb, &c.,) aor. yaguwru , (S, &c.,) inf. n. gaworN (S, K) and guw^uwrN ; (K;) and ↓ AgAr , (Fr, Msb,) inf. n. A_igaArapN ; (K;) but IAth says that this form of the verb is of rare occurrence, (TA,) and As disallows it; (S, Msb, TA;) and ↓ gw~r , inf. n. tagowiyrN ; (S, K;) and ↓ tgw~r ; (K, TA;) He came to the gawor , (As, Fr, IAar, S, Msb, K,) i. e., low land or country, (Msb,) [or the region so called, in Arabia: ] or gAr signifies he journeyed in the region of the gwr : (As, TA:) or gAr and ↓ AgAr signify he took his way towards the gawor . (TA.) There is a difference of opinion respecting the saying of El-Aashà, nabiY~N yaraY maA laA tarawona wa*ikoruhu laEamoriY fiY AlbilaAdi waA^anojadaA ↓ A^agaAra [meaning, accord. to the first explanation of AgAr , A prophet who seeth what ye see not, and whose fame has come to the low lands, by my life, or by my religion, in the several regions, and has come to the high lands ]: As says that AgAr signifies has gone quickly; and Anjd , has risen; and that the poet does not mean has come to the low lands nor to the high lands; holding gAr only to signify the coming to the low land: but Fr asserts that AgAr is a dial. var. of gAr ; and cites this verse as authority: and some say AgAr wAnjd , but when they do not conjoin the two verbs they say gAr ; like as they say hanaA^aniY AlT~aEaAmu wamaraA^aniY , but when they do not conjoin these two verbs they say A^amoraA^aniY : (S:) As also mentions another relation of the second hemistich, commencing AgAm [app. a mistake for A^aqaAma or some other word]: (IKtt:) and there is another relation, accord. to which the second hemistich is maxoruwm , commencing with gaAra . (L.) You say also gaAra waA^anojada meaning (assumed tropical:) He became famous in the low countries and the high. (A in art. njd .) ― -b2- gAr fiY $aYo'K , inf. n. gaworN and guw^uwrN (K) and giyaArN , (Sb, K,) He, or it, entered [or entered deeply ] into a thing. A_igaArapN (S, Mgh, Msb) and gaArapN , (Mgh,) or the latter is a simple subst., [or quasi-inf. n.,] (Msb,) He hastened, (K,) or was quick, (Msb,) in walking, or marching, or journeying: (Msb, K:) he was quick, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) and pushed, or pressed, on, or forward, ( dafaEa , S,) in his running; (S, Mgh, Msb;) said of a horse, (Mgh, Msb,) and of a fox: (S, Mgh:) he (a horse, K) ran vehemently, and was quick, (S, K,) in a gaArap [or raid, or sudden attack upon a people, or their dwellings, ] &c. (K.) (TA. [See also 2 in art. $rq .]) Hence also the saying, A^agaAra A_igaArapa Alv~aEolabi He was quick, and pushed, or pressed, on, or forward, like as does the fox. definition: A cave, or cavern;
sourceDefinition: A cave, or cavern; syn. kahofN ; (S, K;) in a mountain; (S;) as also ↓ magaArapN and ↓ magaArN (S, K) and ↓ mugaArapN and ↓ mugaArN and ↓ gaworN : (K: [but gaArN in this sense is omitted in the CK:]) or what resembles a khf in a mountain, [ only differing in being less large, ] like a sarab : (TA:) or what is hewn out in a mountain, resembling a magaArap : when it is large, or spacious, it is called khf : (Msb:) or what resembles a house, or chamber, in a mountain: (Lh, K:) or a low, or depressed, place in a mountain: (Th, K:) or any low, or depressed, land, country, or ground: (K:) see also gaworN [and xaworN ]: or the hole, or burrow, to which a wild animal betakes itself: (K: [see an instance in art. smw , conj. 8:]) and sometimes ↓ magaArN is applied to the coverts of gazelles, among trees: (S:) the dim. of gaArN is guwayorN : (S, K:) [of which see two exs. (a prov. and a verse) voce buw^osN :] and the pl. (of pauc., TA) A^agowaArN (IJ, K) and (of mult., TA) giyraAnN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- Also The portion of the upper part of the mouth which is behind the faraA$ap [or thin bone of the palate]: or the hollow ( A^uxoduwd ) which is between the two jaws: or the interior of the mouth: (K: [for daAxila Alfami , in the CK, I read daAxilu Alfm , as in the TA:]) or, as some say, the two parts whereof each is called niToEN , [app. meaning the anterior part of the palate and the corresponding part next the lower gums, ] in the HanakaAni [or the palate and the part corresponding to it below ]. (TA.) ― -b3- And AlgaAraAni signifies The [ sockets of the eyes; or] two bones in which are the eyes. (ISd, K.) ― -b4- And The belly and the pudendum: (S:) or the mouth and the pudendum. (K.) Hence the saying of a poet, yasoEaY ligaArayohi [ He works, or earns, for his belly, or his mouth, and his pudendum ]. (S, TA.) -A2- Also ( gaArN ) An army: (S, K:) or a numerous army. (TA.) You say AilotaqaY AlgaAraAni The two armies met. (S.) ― -b2- And A company, or body, of men: (TA:) or a numerous company or body of men. (ISd, K.) -A3- And I. q. gayorapN , (S,) or giyrapN . (K.) [See 1, last signification.] -A4- And A kind of tree, (S, Mgh, K,) of large size, (Mgh, K,) having leaves longer than those of the xilaAf , (Mgh, TA,) and a fruit [or berry ] smaller than the hazel-nut, which is black, and which, being divested of its covering, discloses a heart that is employed in medicine [ that is designed to produce a narcotic or an intoxicating effect: the berries are called Hab~u AlgaAri ]: its leaves have a sweet odour, (Mgh, TA,) and are employed in perfume: (TA:) its fruit is called [ in Persian ] dahomasot : (Mgh, TA:) and it has an oil, (K,) which is called duhonu AlgaAri : (S:) [it is the bay-tree; or female laurel-tree; the laurus nobilis; also called the sweet bay; of which there are several sorts, as the broad-leaved bay, the narrow-leaved bay, &c.: it is commonly supposed to be the laurus of the ancients:] n. un. with p . (TA.) ― -b2- And The leaves of the grapevine. (K.)

sourceDefinition: A garden: (S, Msb:) so in the Greek language [ παράδεισος ]: (M:) or a garden comprising everything that is in gardens: (Zj, M, A, O, K:) such is the proper signification; (Zj, M, O;) and so with the people of every language: (Zj, M:) and containing grape-vines: (Fr, O, K:) or a garden in which are grape-vines: (IAmb, M, Msb:) or a place in which are grape-vines: (TA:) or an ample, beautiful garden: (A:) or a garden comprising grape-vines and palm-trees: (Bd in xviii. 107:) or with the Arabs it signifies a valley abounding with herbage, like a garden: (M:) or a valley, (Zj, Msb,) or valleys, (O, K,) producing various sorts of plants or herbage: (Zj, O, Msb, K:) in the K, for AlA^awodiyapu Al~atiY tunobitu , we should read mina AlA^awodiyapi Al~atiY tunobitu ; (TK;) [or rather, mina AlA^awodiyapi maA yunobitu , as in the Msb:] or a meadow; syn. rawoDapN : (Seer, M:) and the greenness of grapes ( A^aEonaAb ), (so in a copy of the M,) or of herbs ( A^aEo$aAb ): (so in the TA:) masc. and fem.: (Msb:) sometimes the latter; (K;) as in the Kur xxiii. 11, because, by Alfirodawosa is there meant Aljan~apa : (O, TA:) it is an Arabic word, (S, O, Msb, K,) accord. to Fr, (S, O, Msb,) occurring in a verse cited voce vawaAbN , which is by Hassán Ibn-Thábit, (O,) derived from farodasapN , meaning “ width ” or “ amplitude, ” (Msb, K, *) accord. to Fr: (Msb:) or it is Greek, (Zj, O, Msb, K,) transferred to the Arabic language; (Zj, O, Msb;) [i. e., arabicised: but as it occurs in the Kur (xviii. 107 and xxiii. 11), this is contr. to the opinion of Esh-Sháfi'ee and others, who deny that any arabicized word occurs therein: (see sunodusN :)] or it is Syriac: (Zj, O, K:) the pl. is faraAdiysu ; (A, TA;) which is applied by the people of Syria to gardens and grape-vines. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (Bd in xviii. 107,) Alfirodawosu [ Paradise: or] a garden of trees, or walled garden, ( HadiyqapN ,) in Aljan~ap [or Paradise ]: (S:) or the highest of the stages of Aljan~ap : (Bd, ubi suprà:) or the middle and highest part of Aljan~ap . (Jel, ibid.)

definition: , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, *) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, *) aor. , (S, Mgh, O, Msb,) and in one dial. , (Msb, TA,) inf. n. farogN and furoqaAnN , (S, O, Msb, K,) the latter of which has a more intensive signification, (TA,) He made a separation, or a distinction, or difference, (Msb, K, TA,) between the two things, (K, * TA,) or between the parts of the two things: (Msb:) relating alike to objects of sight and to objects of mental perception: (TA:) IAar, by exs. that he mentions, makes it to relate particularly to objects of the mind, such as sayings; and ↓ fr~q , to persons, or material things: (Msb: [and it is stated in the Mgh that the same distinction is mentioned by Az:]) others, however, state that the two verbs are syn.; but that the latter has an intensive signification. (Msb.) It is said in the Kur [v. 28], faA@foruqo bayonanaA wabayona A@loqawomi AlfaAsiqiyna [ Therefore decide Thou, or make Thou a distinction, between us and the unrighteous people ]: accord. to one reading, faA@foriqo . (Msb, TA.) fiyhaA yuforaqu kul~u A^amorK HakiymK , in the Kur [xliv. 3], means [ Wherein ] is made distinct [ every firm decree ]: (Lth, TA:) or is decided; (O, K, TA;) thus expl. by Katádeh. (O, TA.) And in the phrase waqurA=nFA faraqonaAhu , (S, O, K, TA,) in the same [xvii. 107], (S, O, TA,) by faraqonaAhu is meant We have made it distinct, (S, O, K, TA,) and rendered it free from defect, (O, K, TA,) and explained the ordinances therein: (TA:) but some read ↓ far~aqonaAhu , meaning We have sent it down in sundry portions, in a number of days. (S, TA.) waA_i*o faraqonaA bikumu A@lobaHora , (O, K, TA,) in the Kur [ii. 47], (O, TA,) means And when we clave because of you the sea; i. q. falaqonaAhu : (O, K, TA:) another reading, ↓ far~aqonaA , meaning we divided into several portions, is mentioned by IJ; but this is unusual. (TA.) It is also said that Alfaroqu is for rectification; and ↓ Alt~aforiyqu , for vitiation: and IJ says that diyonahumo ↓ A_in~a A@l~a*iyna far~aquwA , in the Kur [vi. 160, and the like occurs in xxx. 31], means Verily those who have divided their religion into sundry parts, and dismembered it, and have disagreed respecting it among themselves: but that some read faraquwA diyonahumo , without teshdeed, meaning, have severed their religion from the other religions [app. by taking it in part, or parts, therefrom ]; or this, he says, may mean the same as the former reading, for sometimes faEala has the same meaning as faE~ala . (TA.) IJ also says that faraqa lahu Eani Al$~aYo'i signifies He made the thing distinct, or plain, to him. definition: , inf. n. taforiyqN and taforiqapN , (S, O, K,) He separated it [ into several, or many, portions ]; disunited it [i. e. a thing, or a collection of things]; or dispersed, or dissipated, it; or did...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taforiyqN and taforiqapN , (S, O, K,) He separated it [ into several, or many, portions ]; disunited it [i. e. a thing, or a collection of things]; or dispersed, or dissipated, it; or did so much [or greatly or widely ]; syn. bad~adahu . (K.) And fr~q bayona AlA^a$oyaA='i [ He made, or caused, a separation &c., or much, or a wide, separation, &c., between the things ]. (Mgh.) [And fiyhimo fr~qhu and Ealayohimo He scattered, or distributed, it among them, and to them. ] See 1, former half, in five places. It is said in a trad. of 'Omar, far~iquwA Eani Almaniy~api waA@joEaluwA Alr~aA^osa raA^osayoni , (Mgh, O, *) meaning Separate ye your cattle by way of preservation from death, [ and make the one head two head, ] by buying two animals with the price of one, that, when one dies, the second may remain. (Mgh, O.) And it is said in a trad. respecting the poor-rate, laA yufar~aqu bayona mujotamiEK walaA yujomaEu bayona mufotariqK There shall be no separating what is put together, nor shall there be a putting together what is separate. (TA. [The reason is, that by either of these acts, in the case of cattle, the amount of the poor-rate may be diminished.]) yufar~iquwna bihi bayona A@lomaro'i wazawojihi [in the Kur ii. 96, meaning Whereby they might dissolve, break up, discompose, derange, disorganize, disorder, or unsettle, the state of union subsisting between the man and his wife, in respect of affairs and of the expression of opinion, or, briefly, whereby they might cause division and dissension between the man and his wife, ] is from Altaforiyqu as meaning ta$otiytu Al$~amoli waAlkalimapi . (El-Isbahánee, TA.) One says also, fr~q AlA^amora , meaning $at~atahu [i. e. He discomposed, deranged, disorganized, disordered, or unsettled, the state of affairs ]. (S in art. $t .) And fr~q EalayonaA AlkalaAma [lit. He scattered speech (app. meaning he jabbered ) at us, or against us ]. (K in art. bq : see R. Q. 1 in that art.) In the saying in the Kur [ii. 130 and iii. 78], laA nufar~iqu bayona A^aHadK minohumo [ We will not make a distinction between any of them ], the verb is allowably made to relate to AHd because this word [in negative phrases] imports a pl. meaning. (TA. [See p. 27, 3rd col.]) See, again, 1, near the middle. -A2- fr~qhu , (O, TA,) inf. n. taforiyqN , (O, K, TA,) also signifies He made him to fear, or be afraid; put him in fear; or frightened him: (O, K, * TA:) and minohu ↓ A^aforaqotuhu I made him to fear, or be afraid of, him, or it: (Msb:) and Lh mentions AlSabiY~a ↓ faraqotu as meaning I frightened the boy, or child; but ISd says, I think it to be far~aqotu . (TA.)

definition: They left their camels in the place of pasture, and did not assist them in bringing forth, nor have them got with young.

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tafar~aqN (O, K) and tifir~aAqN , (K, TA,) with two kesrehs, but accord. to the “ Nawádir ” of Lh taforiyqN , (TA,) [and in the CK taforAq ,] It was, or became, separated, or disunited: or separated much, or greatly, or widely, or into several, or many, portions; or dispersed, or dissipated: contr. of tajam~aEa : and ↓ Aftrq signifies the same: (K, TA:) and so does ↓ Anfrq : (TA:) all are quasi-pass. of far~aqotuhu : (S, * TA:) [or rather the second and third have the former of the meanings mentioned above: and tfr~q has the latter of those meanings:] or ↓ AifotaraqaA is said of two sayings, as quasi-pass. of faraqotu bayonahumaA : and tafar~aqaA , of two men, as quasi-pass. of far~aqotu bayonahamaA : (Mgh, * Msb, TA:) so says IAar: (Msb:) [but] one says also, Aftrq Alqawomu [ The party, or company of men, became separated; or they separated themselves: ] (Msb:) and Esh-Sháfi'ee has used ↓ AifotaraqaA as relating to two persons buying and selling; (Msb, TA;) and so have Ahmad [Ibn-Hambal] and Aboo-Haneefeh and Málik and others. (TA.) It is said in a trad., Albay~aEaAni biAlxiyaAri maA yatafar~aqaA i. e. [ The buyer and seller have the option to annul their contract] as long as they have not become separated bodily; (Mgh, Msb;) originally, maA lamo yatafar~aqo A^abodaAnuhumaA ; for this is the proper meaning. (Msb.) tafar~aqato bihimu AlT~uruqu [properly The roads became separate with them, ] means every one of them went one [ separate ] way. (TA.) [And one says, tfr~qt AlA^agoSaAnu (S in art. $*b , &c.,) The branches were, or became, or grew out, apart, one from another; divaricated; diverged; forked; straggled; or spread widely and dispersedly. And tfr~q A^amoruhu His affair, or state of affairs, became discomposed, deranged, disorganized, disordered, or unsettled, so that he considered what might be its issues, or results, saying at one time, I will do thus, and at another time, I will do thus: see A^ajomaEa ; and $at~a : and ↓ Aftrq signifies the same: see an ex. voce fa$aA , in art. f$w . And tfr~qt kalimatuhumo (K voce $aAla , in art. $wl ,) Their expression of opinion was, or became, discordant: and tfr~qt A=raAw^uhumo Their opinions were, or became, so. ]

definition: A piece, or portion, that is split from a thing, or cleft therefrom;
sourceDefinition: A piece, or portion, that is split from a thing, or cleft therefrom; (S, O, K;) whence its usage in the Kur xxvi. 63: (S, O:) and a portion of anything (K, TA) when it is separated; and the pl. is firaqN : (TA:) or a portion that is separated, or dispersed, of a thing; and thus it is said to mean in the Kur ubi suprá; and the pl. is A^aforaAqN , like A^aHomaAlN as pl. of HimolN . (Msb.) See also firoqapN . ― -b2- Also A great flock or herd, of sheep or goats: (S, O, K:) and (as some say, TA) of the bovine kind: or of gazelles: or of sheep, or goats, only: or of straying sheep or goats; as also ↓ fariyqN , (K, TA,) and ↓ fariyqapN : (TA:) or less than a hundred, (K, TA,) of sheep or goats. (TA.) firoqaAni mino TayorK SawaAf~a , occurring in a trad., in which the second and third chapters of the Kur-án are likened thereto, (L,) means Two flocks [ of birds expanding their wings without moving them in flight ]. (L, TA: but the first word, in both, is without any vowel-sign.) See, again, firoqapN . ― -b3- And A set of boys. (O, K.) An Arab of the desert said of some boys whom he saw, h`w^ulaA='i firoqu sawo'K [ These are a bad set of boys ]. (O.) ― -b4- And A distinct quantity of date-stones with which the camel is fed. (K.) ― -b5- [And app. Any feed for one's beast: see an ex. in art. jl , conj. 4.] -A2- Also A mountain. (IAar, O, K.) And A [ hill, or mountain, or the like, such as is termed ] haDobap . (IAar, O, K.) ― -b2- And A wave, billow, or surge. (IAar, O, K.) ― -b3- And Alfiroqu is the name applied by the Arabs to The star [a] upon the right shoulder of Cepheus. (Kzw.)

definition: Wideness of the space between the two central incisors, (IKh, S, O, K, TA,) of a man: (TA:) and likewise between the two toe-nails of the camel.
sourceDefinition: Wideness of the space between the two central incisors, (IKh, S, O, K, TA,) of a man: (TA:) and likewise between the two toe-nails of the camel. (Yaakoob, S, O, K, TA.) And A division in the Eurof [or comb ] of the cock: and likewise in the forelock, and in the beard, of a man: (S, O, K:) pl. A^aforaAqN . (S, O.) And sparseness, or a scattered state, of the plants, or herbage, of a land. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- In a horse, The state of the hips when one of them is more prominent than the other; which is disapproved: (S, O, K, TA:) or a deficiency in one of the thighs, in comparison with the other: or a deficiency in one of the hips. (TA.) ― -b3- Also The dawn: or Alfaraqu signifies falaqu AlS~uboHi : (K:) or what has broken of the bright gleam of dawn; of the dawn that rises and spreads, filling the horizon with its whiteness; ( maA A@nofalaqa mino Eamuwdi AlS~uboHi [which is one of the explanations of Alfalaqu in the K];) because it has become separated from the blackness of the night: (TA:) one says, A^aboyanu mino faraqi AlS~uboHi a dial. var. of falaqi AlS~uboHi [i. e. More distinct than what has broken of the bright gleam of dawn ]. (S, O, Msb, * TA.) -A2- It is also the inf. n. of fariqa [q. v.: when used as a simple subst., signifying Fear, or fright ]. (S, O, Msb.) -A3- Also, and ↓ faroqN , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) the latte accord. to the usage of the relaters of traditions, (Az, Mgh, O, Msb, TA,) but the former accord. to the usage of the Arabs, (Az, Mgh, O, * TA,) or the former is the more chaste (K, TA) accord. to Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà and Khálid Ibn-Yezeed, (TA,) A certain vessel, (T, Mgh, O, Msb,) a measure of capacity, (S, O, K, TA,) of large size, (TA,) well known, (S,) in El-Medeeneh, (S, Msb, K,) holding three A=SuE [a pl. of SaAEN ], (Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA,) or, (K, [app. referring to ↓ faroqN only,]) which is the same quantity, sixteen pints, (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K, * TA,) i. e. twelve times the quantity termed mud~ by the people of El-Hijáz: (TA:) or, accord. to El-Kutabee, the ↓ faroq is sixteen pints, and the SAE is one third of the faroq ; but the faraq is eighty pints: or the ↓ faroq , he adds, is, as some say, four pints: (Mgh:) or it is four A^arobaAE [pl. of ruboEN , q. v.]; (K, TA;) thus accord. to AHát: and IAth says, the faraq is said to be five A^aqosaAT ; [or six; (see qisoTN ;)] the qisoT being the half of a SAE : but the ↓ faroq is a hundred and twenty pints: (TA:) in the “ Nawádir ” of Hishám, on the authority of [the Imám] Mohammad, the ↓ faroq is said to be thirty-six pints; but [Mtr says] this I have not found in any of the lexicons in my possession; and so what is said in the Moheet, that it is sixty pints: (Mgh:) the pl. is furoqaAnN , (S, Mgh, O, K, TA,) which is of ↓ faroqN and of faraqN ; (S, Mgh, O, TA;) and A^aforuqN occurs in a trad. as a pl. [of pauc.] of faraqN meaning the measure thus called. (TA.) 'Áïsheh is related to have said that she and the Prophet used to wash themselves from a vessel called the ↓ faroq . (O, Msb.) [In a verse of which a hemistich is cited in the S and TA, the pl. furoqaAn is used as meaning Milking-vessels. (See also Alfuroqu .) Respecting a modern signification of ↓ faroq ( A bale, or sack, of merchandise), see De Sacy's Chrest. Ar., sec. ed., iii., 378-9 and 382.]

definition: , originally an inf.
sourceDefinition: , originally an inf. n. (Msb. [See 1, first sentence.]) Anything that makes a separation, or distinction, between truth and falsity. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) AlfuroqaAnu signifies The Kur-án; (S, O, Msb, K;) as also ↓ Alfuroqu . (S, O, K.) ― -b3- And The Book of the Law revealed to Moses, (Az, O, K,) in which a distinction is made between that which is allowable and that which is forbidden. (O.) ― -b4- And Proof, evidence, or demonstration. (O, K.) ― -b5- And The time a little before daybreak: (AA, O, K:) or the dawn. (O, K.) One says, TalaEa AlfuroqaAnu [ The dawn rose ]. (O.) ― -b6- And Aid, or victory: (IDrd, O, K:) so, accord. to IDrd, in the phrase yawoma AlfuroqaAni in the Kur [viii. 42]: (O:) or by this phrase is meant The day of Bedr, (O, K,) in which a distinction was made between right and wrong. (O.) ― -b7- And The cleaving of the sea: so it means [accord. to some] in the Kur ii. 50. (O, K.) ― -b8- And Boys: (O, K:) such the people of the olden time used to make witnesses [in law-suits or the like]. (O.) -A2- It is also pl. of faroqN (S, M, O, K) and of faraqN . (S, Mgh, O.)

definition: A TaAy^ifap [or party, &c.
sourceDefinition: A TaAy^ifap [or party, &c.,] (S, Msb, K) more in number, (S, K, *) or larger, (Msb,) than a firoqap : (S, Msb, K:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aforiqapN and [of mult.] A^aforiqaA='u and furuwqN (K, TA) and furuqN : (CK:) see also firoqapN , in two places; and see firoqN : AHei says that it is itself a quasi-pl. n., applied to few and to many: 'Abd-el-Hakeem, that it occurs in the sense of a TaAy^ifap [or party, &c.], and in the sense of a single man: and El-Isbahánee, that it signifies a company of men apart from others [i. e. a party of men ]: (MF, TA:) or [simply] a company [ of men ]. (O.) ― -b2- And A separator of himself. (IB, TA.) Hence the saying, huwa A^asoraEu mino fariyqi Alxayoli i. e. [ He is swifter ] than the outgoer, or outrunner, of the horses. (TA.) ― -b3- niy~apN farayqN means mufar~iqN [i. e. A place to which one purposes journeying that separates widely ]: a poet says, A^aHaq~N A^an~a jiyoratanaA A@sotaqal~uwA faniy~atunaA waniy~atuhumo fariyqu [ Is it true that our neighbours have gone away, so that the place to which we purpose journeying and the place to which they purpose journeying are such as separate widely ]: he says fariyq in like manner as one applies [the epithet] SadiyqN to a company of men. (Sb, TA.) -A2- Also A palm-tree ( naxolapN ) in which is [app. meaning out of which grows ] another. (AA, AHn, O, TA.)

definition: , applied to a man and to a woman, (IDrd, S, O, K,) and having no pl.
sourceDefinition: , applied to a man and to a woman, (IDrd, S, O, K,) and having no pl., (S, O,) and ↓ far~uwqapN , applied to a man (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K) and to a woman, (K,) and ↓ faAruwqapN , applied to a man (O, K,) and to a woman, or, as epithets applied to a man, faruwqapN , (K,) and ↓ far~uwqapN , (CK,) and ↓ faAruwqapN , and ↓ faruwqN , (K,) but this last is also applied to a woman, (IB, TA,) and ↓ far~uwqN , and ↓ faAruwqN , One who fears much, or vehemently; [or rather the epithets with the affix p are doubly intensive, meaning one who fears very much; ] (S, * O, * K, TA;) and ↓ fariqN and ↓ faruqN signify the same as the other epithets above; or ↓ faruqN signifies fearing, or fearful, by nature; and ↓ fariqN , [simply,] fearing a thing. (K.) It is said in a prov., rub~a EajalapK tahabu rayovFA warub~a faruwqapK yudoEaY layovFA warub~a gayovK lamo yakuno gayovFA [ Many an act of haste causes (lit. gives ) slowness, and many a very fearful man is called a lion, and many a collection of clouds has not been productive of rain ]: (S, * O:) said by Málik Ibn-'Amr Ibn-Mohallam, when Leyth, his brother, looked hopefully at the clouds from afar, and desired to avail himself of the benefit thereof; whereupon Málik said to him, “ Do not, for I fear for thee some of the troops of the Arabs: ” but he disobeyed him, and journeyed with his family; and he had not stayed [away] a little while when he came [back], and his family had been taken. (O. [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 535.]) -A2- And Alfaruwqapu signifies AlHuromapu [meaning Honour, or reputation; or that which one is under an obligation to respect and defend ]: (O, K, TA: [in the CK AlHuzomapu :]) so Sh was told: and [so, app., ↓ Alfaruwqu , for] he cites as an ex., maA zaAla Eanohu Humoquhu wamuwquhu waAll~uw^omu Hat~aY A@notuhikato faruwqahu [ His foolishness and his stupidity quitted him not, and meanness, so that his honour, &c., was violated ]. (O, TA.) -A3- And The fat of the kidneys: (O, K:) so says A'Obeyd, on the authority of El-Umawee; but Sh disallowed this meaning, and knew it not. (O, TA.)

definition: [act. part. n. of faraqa , q. v.]. AlfaAriqaAtu , mentioned in the Kur lxxvii. 4, means Those angels that descend with what makes a distinction between truth and falsity: (Fr, O, K:) or that...
sourceDefinition: [act. part. n. of faraqa , q. v.]. AlfaAriqaAtu , mentioned in the Kur lxxvii. 4, means Those angels that descend with what makes a distinction between truth and falsity: (Fr, O, K:) or that distinguish between that which is allowable and that which is forbidden: (Th, TA:) or that make a distinction between things according as God has commanded them. (Er-Rághib, TA.) ― -b2- Also, faAriqN , A she-camel, and a she-ass, in consequence of her being taken with the pains of parturition, going away at random in the land; (S, O, K;) and so faAriqapN , as in the “ Mufradát: ” or a she-camel that separates herself from her mate, and brings forth alone: or a she-camel that runs ( ta$otad~u ), and then casts her young one by reason of the pain that befalls her; thus expl. by IAar: (TA:) pl. fawaAriqu and fur~aqN (S, O, K) and furuqN (K) and fur~aAqN , which is thus used by El-Aashà, applied to she-camels, and ↓ mafaAriyqu is [an irreg. pl.] likewise applied to she-camels as syn. with fawaAriqu . (TA.) ― -b3- And hence, as being likened to such a she-camel, applied to a cloud ( saHaAbapN ) as meaning (tropical:) Apart from the other clouds; (S, O, K;) cut off from the main aggregate of the clouds: (ISd, TA:) or an isolated cloud, that will not break its promise [ of giving rain ], and sometimes preceded by thunder and lighting: (TA:) thus applied, also, having for pl. fawaAriqu and fur~aqN [&c.]. (O.)

definition: A thing that makes a distinction between two things: and a man who makes a distinction between truth and falsity: (TA:) or one who makes a distinction between affairs, or cases.
sourceDefinition: A thing that makes a distinction between two things: and a man who makes a distinction between truth and falsity: (TA:) or one who makes a distinction between affairs, or cases. (TA.) -A2- See also faruwqapN , first sentence.

definition: [ Sundry, or separate, or scattered, portions or things: and sundry times ].
sourceDefinition: [ Sundry, or separate, or scattered, portions or things: and sundry times ]. You say, A^axa*otu Haq~iY minohu biAlt~afaAriyqi (S, O, K, * TA) i. e. [ I took my right, or due, from him in sundry portions: or] at sundry times. (TA.) And Dam~a tafaAriyqa mataAEihi i. e. [ He put together ] what were scattered [ of his household goods, or furniture and utensils ]. (TA.) A_in~aka xayorN mino tafaAriyqi AlEaSaA [ Verily thou art better than the several portions of the staff ], (S, O, K,) which is a prov., (O,) was said by a poet, (S,) or by Ghaneeyeh, (O,) or Ghuneiyeh, (K,) El-Aarábeeyeh, to her son; for he was evil in disposition, [ EAzimFA in the CK is a mistake for EaArimFA ,] very mischievous, notwithstanding his weakness, (O, K,) and slenderness of bone; (O;) and he assaulted one day a young man, who thereupon cut off his nose, and his mother took the mulct for it; so her condition became good after abasing poverty; then he assaulted another, who cut off his ear; and another, who cut off his lip; and his mother took the mulct for each; and when she saw the goodness of her condition, (O, K,) the camels and the sheep or goats and the household goods that she had acquired, (O,) she said thus: (O, K:) for from the staff (S, O, K) when it is broken (S) is made a saAjuwr [q. v.], and from this are made tent-pegs, and from the tent-peg is made an EiraAn [q. v.], and from this are made tawaAdK [pl. of tawodiyapN , q. v.]. (S, O, K.)

definition: (S, O, K) and maforiqN (S, O, Msb, K) The middle of the head;
sourceDefinition: (S, O, K) and maforiqN (S, O, Msb, K) The middle of the head; (S, O, K;) the place where the hair of the head is separated: (S, O, Msb, K:) pl. mafaAriqu ; which is used also in the sense of the sing., as though the sing. applied to every part thereof: (S, O:) one says, $aAbato mafaAriqu raA^osihi [meaning The place (lit. places ) of the separation of the hair of his head became white, or hoary ]. (Mgh voce *akarN .) [See also faroqN .] ― -b2- Also The place, of a road, where another road branches off: (S, O, Msb, K:) both words are used in this sense likewise: (S, O, K: *) pl. as above. (K.) ― -b3- And [hence] one says, waqafotuhu EalaY mafaAriqi AlHadiyvi (tropical:) [ I made him to know ] the modes, or manners, [ of the narrative, or discourse, ] or the manifest, plain, or obvious, modes or manners [ thereof ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. faloHN , He clave, split, slit, or cracked; and he cut: (K: [compare falaja , and falaqa , and fala*a :]) he clave, and cut, iron. (T, Msb.) Hence, the saying of a poet, (T, TA,) A_in~a AlHadiyda biAlHadiydi yufolaHu Verily iron with iron is cloven, and cut. (T, S, Mgh, * K. *) And falaHa raA^osahu , inf. n. as above, He clave, split, or cracked, his head. (TA.) And falaHa $afatahu , aor. and inf. n. as above, He slit, or cracked, his lip. (L.) And falaHa AlA^aroDa , (S, Msb,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (Msb.) He furrowed, or ploughed, the land, to cultivate it; he tilled the ground. (S, Msb. [And falajahaA has a similar meaning.]) -A2- Also, aor. and inf. n. as above, He acted with artifice, fraud, or guile; (K, TA;) and so ↓ fl~H , inf. n. tafoliyHN . (K, TA.) You say, bihimo ↓ fl~H He acted with artifice, fraud, or guile, towards them, and said what was not true. (TA.) And bihi ↓ fl~H He mocked at him, or derided him, and acted with artifice, fraud, or guile, towards him. (L, K. *) ― -b2- And, aor. as above, inf. n. faloHN and falaAHapN , He defrauded him in a sale; syn. of the inf. n. baxosN fiY bayoEK : (so in the CK:) or he bade high for an article of merchandise in order to inveigh another into purchasing it at a high price: syn. of the inf. n. najo$N fiY bayoEK . (So in other copies of the K, and in the L and TA.) You say, falaHa bihi [ He so acted towards him in a sale ]: this is when one trusts to thee, and says to thee, “ Sell to me a slave, ” or “ an article of merchandise, ” or “ buy it for me, ” and thou comest to the merchants, and buyest it at a high price, and sellest by defrauding, and obtainest something from the merchant: or, accord. to the T, faloHN signifies a hirer's exceeding [ in an offer ] in order that another may do so; thus inciting him. (L.) -A3- faliHato $afatuhu Als~ufolaY , [aor. ,] inf. n. falaHN , His under lip was slit, or cracked. (MA.) See also falaHN below.

definition: He prospered; was successful; attained, or acquired, that which he desired or sought, (MA, L, Msb,) or what was good, or felicity, or that whereby he became in a happy and good state: (L:) he was, or...
sourceDefinition: He prospered; was successful; attained, or acquired, that which he desired or sought, (MA, L, Msb,) or what was good, or felicity, or that whereby he became in a happy and good state: (L:) he was, or became, fortunate, happy, or in a happy and good state. (MA.) It is commonly known as an intrans. verb; but Talhah Ibn-Musarrif and 'Amr Ibn-'Obeyd, read qado A^ufoliHa A@lomuw^ominuwna , [the first verse of ch. xxiii. of the Kur-án,] with the verb in the pass. form. (MF.) [See also 10.] ― -b2- He was, or became, in a state of safety. (L.) ― -b3- He continued in a good, or prosperous, state, (MA, L,) and in the enjoyment of ease, comfort, or the blessings of life. (L.) ― -b4- AflH biAl$~aYo'i He lived [or continued in life ] by means of the thing. (K.) The saying of 'Abeed, A^afoliHo bimaA $iy^ota faqado yubolagu biA@ waqado yuxad~aEu AlA^ariybu The Perseus transcribers were unclear about the last character of line one and the first character of line two. means Live thou by what thou wilt: whether by stupidity or by intelligence; for [ one's object is sometimes attained by stupidity, and the intelligent, or sagacious, is sometimes deluded, or much deluded; or] the stupid is sometimes supplied with the means of subsistence, and the intelligent is [ sometimes ] denied: (T, L:) or the meaning is prosper thou, &c. (L.)

And Continuance, or permanence, in a good, or prosperous, state, (A, L, K,) and in the enjoyment of ease, comfort, or the blessings of life; and the continuance of good: (L:) and simply continuance, permanence, lastingness, duration, or endurance. (L.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, L, K,) inf. n. qaradN , (S, L), It (wool) fell off by degrees from the sheep, and became compacted in lumps, or clotted: (S:) or it (wool, L, and hair, L, K) became contracted together, (L, K,) and knotted in its extremities; (L;) as also ↓ tqr~d . (L, K.) ― -b2- It (a tanned skin) became worm-eaten. (S, K.) -A2- (tropical:) He (a man) was, or became, silent by reason of impotence of speech; (S, K;) as also ↓ Aqrd and ↓ qr~d : (K:) or he was, or became, abject, and humble, or submissive: or, acc. to IAar ↓ Aqrd signifies he (a man) was, or became, silent by reason of abjectness: [see also xrida :] or, acc. to another, he was, or became, still and abject. definition: [a coll. gen. n.] Refuse of wool; (L, K;) afterwards applied also to soft hair ( wabar ), and other hair, and flax: (L:) or soft hair and wool that fall off by degrees from the animals, and become...
sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n.] Refuse of wool; (L, K;) afterwards applied also to soft hair ( wabar ), and other hair, and flax: (L:) or soft hair and wool that fall off by degrees from the animals, and become compacted in lumps, or clotted: (L, K:) or refuse of wool, and what falls off by degrees from the sheep, and becomes compacted in lumps, or clotted: (S:) or bad wool: (R:) or the worst of wool and soft hair, and what is picked up thereof from the ground: (Nh:) a piece thereof is termed qaradapN . (S.) It is said in a proverb, Eakarato EalaY Algazoli biA^axarapK falamo tadaEo binajodK qaradapN , Eakarato meaning EaTafato , [ She returned to spinning at last, and left not in Nejd a piece of refuse of wool ]: (S, L:) in the K, Eavarato is put for Eakarato ; and both readings are mentioned by the relaters of proverbs: [ Evrt ElY Algzl app. signifies she applied herself by chance to spinning:] the proverb is applied to him who neglects a needful business when it is possible, and seeks to accomplish it when it is beyond his reach: (K:) its origin is the fact, that a woman neglects spinning while she finds that which she may spin, (of cotton or flax &c., L,) until, when it is beyond her reach, she seeks for refuse of wool among sweepings and rubbish. (L, K.) ― -b2- Also, Palmbranches stripped of their leaves: n. un. with p . (K.) ― -b3- Also, A thing like down, sticking to the [ plant called ] Turovuwv . (K.) ― -b4- Also, Little things, [i. e., little flocks of clouds, ] less than [ what are termed ] saHaAb [or clouds in the common acceptation of the term ] not conjoined; as also ↓ mutaqar~idN ; (K;) in some copies of the K ↓ mutaqar~idapN . (TA.) See also qaridN . -A2- Also, A hesitation in speech; (El-Hejeree, L, K;) because a man who hesitates in his speech is silent respecting somewhat of that which he would say. (L.) See also qarida .

sourceDefinition: and qisoTaAsN A balance, or instrument for weighing: (S, Msb, K; and Bd in xvii. 37:) or the most even and most just kind thereof: or such as is just, of whatever kind it be: (K:) or i. q. qab~aAnN [ a steelyard ]: or, as Lth thinks, the iron of the qb~An : or i. q. $aAhiynN [the beam of a balance ]: (TA:) or i. q. farasoTuwnN [an arabicized Persian word, signifying a public standard of weights or measures ]: (Zj, TA:) also written qSTAs : (K:) said to be Arabic, from AlqisoTu , meaning “ justice: ” (Msb:) or a Greek word arabicized; (IDrd, Msb, K;) and its being so does not impugn the truth of the Kur-án's being [altogether] Arabic; for when a foreign word is used by the Arabs, and made by them conformable with their language in respect of desinential syntax and determinateness and indeterminateness and the like, it becomes Arabic: (Bd, ubi supra:) pl. qasaATiysu . (Msb.)

definition: The sheath of the penis (S, A, O, K) of a beast, or of a solid-hoofed animal, (K,) [i.
sourceDefinition: The sheath of the penis (S, A, O, K) of a beast, or of a solid-hoofed animal, (K,) [i. e.] of the horse, (S, A, O,) and of other than the horse (S, O) among the solid-hoofed; (S;) or originally, of the solid-hoofed, and afterwards used in relation to others, as of the camel. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] qunobu AlA^asadi , i. e. (assumed tropical:) The sheath of the penis of the Lion, is a name by which the Arabs call the star [b] upon the hinder part of the tail of Leo: [this, is should be observed, is the place of the star in the figure of Leo commonly known; but the ancient Arabs, or many of them, extended the figure of that constellation (as they did also that of Scorpio) far beyond the limits which we assign to it: (see Al*~iraAEu :) another meaning of qunob in relation to a lion, which will be found below, may perhaps be intended in this case, but I think it unlikely:] the Arabs also called the same star AlS~arofapu [q. v.]. (Kzw.) ― -b3- [Hence, likewise,] qunobN signifies also (tropical:) The baZor of a woman; (K;) [meaning the prepuce of the clitoris; as being likened to a qunob properly so called; i. e.] it is metonymically [thus] applied to the part that is circumcised, of a woman. (JK, A.) ― -b4- See also qinaAbN , in two places. -A2- Also A large sail, (O, K,) one of the greatest of the sails of a ship. (O.)

definition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and qun~abN (K) [ Cannabis, or hemp;
sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and qun~abN (K) [ Cannabis, or hemp; ] i. q. A^abaqN [a less-known word]; a genuine Arabic word; (S, O;) or, accord. to AHn, a Pers. word [ kanabN ] which has become current in the language of the Arabs; (Mgh;) vulgarly pronounced qin~ib ; (TA;) [loosely expl. as] a sort of kat~aAn [or flax ], (K, TA,) i. e. the coarse [ sort ], of which are made ropes and the like; (TA;) a plant of which the skin, or rind, is twisted into ropes; (Msb;) its stems are bruised until the culms becomes strewn in fragments and the rind thereof becomes detached; and one says HibaAlu Alqin~abi [ the ropes of hemp ]: (AHn, Mgh:) it has a grain called $ahodaAnaj [q.v.]: (Mgh, Msb:) ↓ qinaAb , [thus without teshdeed,] occurring in a verse of Aboo-Heiyeh En-Numeyree, is said to signify the same as qin~ab ; but whether it be a dial. var. or altered therefrom [by poetic license] is doubtful. (L, TA.) [See also De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, sec. ed., i. 269.]

definition: and (sometimes, S, Msb) kirosiY~N (S, Msb, K) A throne;
sourceDefinition: and (sometimes, S, Msb) kirosiY~N (S, Msb, K) A throne; syn. sariyrN : (K:) a chair: (TK:) a seat not larger than is sufficient for one person: (Bd, ii. 256:) [and a stool: ] pl. karaAsiY~N (S, Msb, K) and sometimes karaAsK , agreeably with a rule mentioned by ISk. (Msb.) It is the place [or seat] of the king, and of the learned man: and hence, as used in the Kur ii. 256, it is explained as signifying (tropical:) Dominion: (A:) and (tropical:) the power of God, whereby He holds the heavens and the earth: (TA:) and (tropical:) knowledge: (A, K:) which last explanation is ascribed to I'Ab: but the truth is, that I'Ab explained it as there signifying the [ foot-stool of God; or] place of the feet: but as to the Earo$ [of God], this is immeasurable: (Az, TA:) or it signifies the sphere of the stars. (TA, art. Er$ .) [Hence, also, you say,] huwa mino A^aholi AlkurosiY~i (tropical:) He is of the people of science. (TK.) [And hence,] AlkaraAsiY~u is also used [elliptically] to signify (tropical:) The learned men; accord. to Ktr. (A.) ― -b2- Also, A prop, or support, for a wall. (TA.) ― -b3- [ *aAtu AlkurosiY~i The Constellation Cassiopeia: see xaDiybN .]

definition: , (L, K,) or laboxN , (as mentioned by AHn.
sourceDefinition: , (L, K,) or laboxN , (as mentioned by AHn., on the authority of another, [but see below,]) [a coll. gen. n., n. un. with p , The persea of Theophrastus and Dioscorides; (De Sacy, “ Relation de l'Egypte par Abd-Allatif, ” in which see a full and learned disquisition respecting this tree, pp. 47 et seqq.)] described to AHn, by a man acquainted with it, as growing at Ansinè, in Upper Egypt, as a kind of large tree, resembling the dulob [or plane-tree ], having a green fruit, resembling the date, very sweet, but disagreeable, excellent for pain in the teeth: when it is sawn, it [meaning the saw-dust] makes blood to flow from the nose of him who saws it: it is sawn into planks, and a plank of it obtains the price of fifty deenárs: it is used in the building of ships: they assert that if two planks of it be strongly attached together, and put in water for a year, they unite, and form one plank: in the T it is not said that they are put in water for a year, nor for less, nor for more: some assert that this tree, in Persia, killed; but when transplanted to Egypt, it became such that [ the fruit of ] it was eaten, without injuring: Ibn-Beytár mentions it. (L, and parts also in the K.) The n. un. is also explained as the name of a certain great tree, like the A^avoA^abap , or greater, the leaves of which resemble those of the walnut-tree ( Aljawoz ), having a fruit like that of the HamaAT , bitter in taste, which, when eaten, excites thirst; and when water is drunk upon it, inflates the belly: it is one of the trees of the mountains. (AHn, L.) [In a verse cited by AHn, the coll. appellation of this latter tree is read labax , with fet-h to the l and b .] [The name of labax is now given in Egypt to a kind of acacia; the mimosa lebbeck of Linnæus: and labaxu Aljabal , to the menispermum leæba of Delile; the leæba of Forskal. See also lubaAjN .]

(Msb.)

definition: What is picked up, or taken from the ground, (S, Msb, K,) of a thing;
sourceDefinition: What is picked up, or taken from the ground, (S, Msb, K,) of a thing; (S, Msb;) as also ↓ luqoTapN and ↓ luqaTapN and ↓ luqaATapN : (K:) or ↓ this last signifies what one picks up, of lost property; as also ↓ luqaATN , with the p elided; and ↓ luqaTapN like ruTabapN : (Msb:) or ↓ luqaATapN signifies also what falls, or drops, of a thing that is worthless, (K, TA,) or paltry, and is taken by any one who chooses to take it: (TA:) and the same, what is picked up from the stumps of the branches of palm-trees, [app. meaning dates picked up thence, ] after the cutting off of the dates: (TA:) IAth says, that ↓ luqaTapN , with damm to the l and fet-h to the q , is often mentioned in trads., and signifies property which is found: (TA:) Az says, that luqaTapN , with fet-h to the q , signifies a thing which one finds dropped, or thrown down, and takes; (Mgh, Msb;) and that all the lexicologists and skilful grammarians say so; (Msb;) and in like manner, A 'Obeyd, on the authority of As and of El-Ahmar; (TA;) only Lth, of all whom he has heard, saying that it is ↓ luqoTapN , with sukoon; (Mgh, Msb;) and Fr: (TA:) IF and ElFárábee and others mention only ↓ luqaTapN ; and some reckon the pronunciation with sukoon as an error of the vulgar; and the reason is this; that the original word is ↓ luqaATapN , which, in consequence of its being in frequent use, as applied to what is picked up in plundering, is contracted, sometimes, by the elision of the p , into ↓ luqaATN , and sometimes, by the elision of the A into ↓ luqaTapN ; and if they made the q quiescent, there would be two alterations in the word, and such double alteration does not exist in chaste language: (Msb:) IB, however, says that ↓ luqoTapN is correct; and he approves it; because fuEolapN has the sense of a pass. part. n., as in the instance of DuHokapN ; and fuEalapN has the sense of an act. part. n., as in the instance of DuHakapN ; and that it occurs in poetry: and IAth observes, that some say thus; but that ↓ luqaTapN is more common and more correct. (TA.) Anything that is scattered, of ears of corn, or of fruit; n. un. with p : (TA:) what is picked up, or taken from the ground, (S, Msb, K,) by men, (S,) of ears of corn; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ luqaATN , with damm: (S:) and ↓ laqaATN , like saHaAbN , the ears of corn which the reaping-hooks miss, (AHn, K,) and which men pick up. (AHn.) What is picked up from a mine: (Msb:) pieces of gold found in a mine; (K;) or such are termed laqaTu maEodinK : (S:) or laqaTN signifies pieces of gold, or of silver, like what are termed $a*or , and larger, in mines; which are the best thereof: and one says *ahabN laqaTN : (Lth:) and ↓ mulotaqaTN , also, signifies gold found in a mine. (TA.) You say also, fiY h`*aA AlmakaAni laqaTN mina AlmarotaEi In this place is some small quantity of pasturage. (S.) And fiY AlA^aroDi laqaTN lilomaAli In the land is pasturage not much in quantity for the beasts. (TA.) The pl. is A^aloqaATN . (TA.)

definition: and in an intensive sense ↓ laq~aATN and [in a doubly intensive sense] ↓ laq~aATapN A man [ who picks up things from the ground;
sourceDefinition: and in an intensive sense ↓ laq~aATN and [in a doubly intensive sense] ↓ laq~aATapN A man [ who picks up things from the ground; and the second, who does so much, or often; and the third, who does so very much, or very often: or] who takes things from places where they were not thought to be: (Msb:) and all signify a man who picks up the ears of corn [ that fall ] when the crop is reaped, and [ the fruit that falls ] when the ripe dates are cut from the raceme: (TA:) and the first and second, a bird that picks up grains. (Msb.) ― -b2- ↓ likul~i saAqiTapK laAqiTapN For every saying that falls from one, there is a person who will take it up: (Msb in art. sqT :) or for every word that falls from the mouth of the speaker, there is a person who will hear it and pick it up and publish it: (S, * K:) a proverb, (TA,) relating to the guarding of the tongue: (K:) the p in lAqTp is to give intensiveness to the meaning, (Msb, in art. sqT ,) or for the purpose of assimilation: (Msb in that art., and in the present one:) if you say likul~i DaAy^iEK , or the like, you say laAqiTN . (Msb in the present art.) ― -b3- AlHaSaY ↓ laAqiTapN The qaAniSap [meaning stomach, &c.,] of a bird, (S, K,) in which pebbles become collected: (S:) or the omasum ( qib~p ) of a sheep or goat [and the corresponding ventricle of a camel, as is shown in the TA in art. HSl ; also called laq~aATapu AlHaSaY (see qurayoHaA='u );] because it conveys thereinto whatever it eats of earth and pebbles; (A, TA;) as also All~aAqiTapN [alone]. (TA.) -A2- laAqiTN also signifies (tropical:) Any freedman, or emancipated slave: (K:) or the slave of a freedman. (S in art. mqT , and TA in art. sqT :) the slave of the lAqT is called maAqiTN ; and the slave of the mAqT is called saAqiTN : and hence the saying, huwa saAqiTu bonu maAqiTi boni laAqiTK . (K, TA [but in the CK, for huwa we find banuw , with the necessary difference in what follows it.]) See art. sqT . ― -b2- See also laqiyTapN : and see A^aloqaATN , which may be a pl. of laAqiTN ; as in luq~aATN , which is explained with A^aloqaATN .

definition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, M,) inf. n. mar~N [and mamar~N ] and muruwrN , (S, M, Msb, K,) He, or it, passed; passed by, or beyond; went; went on; proceeded; passed, or went, along, or through, or over; went away; passed away; syn. jaAza ; (M, K;) and *ahaba ; (S, M, Msb, K;) and maDaY ; (A, Mgh;) as also ↓ Astmr~ . (S, A, Mgh, K.) You say, mar~a Alr~ajulu , (TK,) and Ald~ahoru , (Msb,) and AlA^amoru ; and ↓ Astmr~ ; (A, Mgh;) The man, (TK,) and time, (Msb,) and the affair, (A, Mgh,) passed; &c. (A, Mgh, Msb, TK.) The saying in the Kur, [vii. 189,] Hamalato HamolFA xafiyfFA famar~ato bihi signifies i. q. bh ↓ Astmr~t , (A, K,) which is another reading, (Bd,) i. e., [ She bore a light burden in her womb, and ] went with it, and moved from place to place, and rose and sat, not being oppressed by its weight: (A:) [or went on with it in the same course or manner: ] or went and came with it, by reason of its lightness: (Jel:) or rose and sat with it, (Zj, Bd,) not being oppressed by its weight: (Zj:) so accord. to both the readings mentioned above: (Bd:) by the burden being meant the impregnating fluid. (Bd, Jel, TA.) ― -b2- [It is also said of water, meaning It ran, or flowed. And one says, mar~ati Alr~iyHu The wind passed along, or blew. ] ― -b3- mar~a bihi , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) and mar~a Ealayohi , (S, A, Msb,) but the former is more common than the latter, (Mughnee, voce bi ,) for which the BenooYarbooa say, mir~a Elyh , with kesr, (TA,) and mar~ahu , [respecting which see what follows the explanation,] (M, K,) aor. , (S,) inf. n. mar~N and mamar~N (S, A, Msb) and muruwrN ; (A, Msb;) and bihi ↓ Aimotar~a , and Aimotar~a Ealayohi ; (M, K;) He passed, or went, by him, or it; syn. AijotaAza , (S, Msb,) or jaAza Ealayohi , (M, K,) or jaAwazahu wa*ahaba . (A.) mar~a may be a verb trans. by means of a particle and without a particle: or in mar~ahu the particle may be suppressed: Jereer says, tamur~uwna Ald~iyaAra walamo taEuwjuwA kalaAmukumu EalaY~a A_i*FA HaraAmu [ Ye pass by the dwellings without turning aside and alighting: the speaking to you is therefore forbidden to me ]: but it is said that the true reading is mararotumo biAld~iyaAri [ Ye have passed by the dwellings ]: which shows that he feared to make the verb trans. without a particle: IAar says, that mar~a zayodFA signifies the same as mar~a bihi [ He passed by Zeyd ], without being elliptical, but as being properly trans.; but IJ, allowing this, says that it is not a phrase commonly obtaining. (M, TA.) ― -b4- [ mar~a Ealayohi also signifies He, or it, passed, or went, along, or over, or across, it. You say, mar~a EalaY Aljisori He passed, or went, along, or over the bridge, or dyke. ] And mar~a Als~ik~iynu EalaY Haloqi Al$~aApi The knife passed across the throat of the sheep, or goat. (Msb.) ― -b5- [Also, It (a period of time) passed over him, or it: and it (a calamity) came upon him: see an ex. of the latter signification below, voce mur~N .] ― -b6- mar~a bihi as syn. with ↓ A^amar~ahu , trans. of mar~a : see 4. -A2- mar~a , aor. and : see 4. ― -b2- mar~ahu , as trans. of mar~a , of which the aor. is : see 2. ― -b3- mur~a His bile, or gall, became roused. (A.) You say murirotu [ I suffered an attack of bile ], from Almir~apu , (T,) or murirotu bihi , (Lh, M, K,) aor. A^umar~u , inf. n. mar~N and mir~apN , (Lh, T, M, K,) the latter of which [in the CK written mar~ap , but in the T, M, &c. mir~ap , and expressly said in the TA to be with kesr,] is also a simple subst., (T,) or, as Lh says in one place, mir~N is the inf. n. and mir~apN is a simple subst., (M, TA,) Bile, or gall, overcame me [ by reason of it: app. referring to food]. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , (inf. n. A_imoraArN , TA,) He made him, or it, to pass, pass by or beyond, go, go away, or pass away; (A, Msb, TA;) as also bihi ↓ mar~a . (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Amr~ Al$~iEora [(assumed tropical:) He recited the poetry, especially, with fluency ]. (K, art. *br .) ― -b3- Amr~hu bihi (in some copies of the K, Amtr~ bh , but the former is the right reading, TA) [and Ealayohi ] He made him, or it, to pass, or go, by him, or it, (K.) ― -b4- Amr~hu EalaY Aljisori He made him to pass, or go, along, or over, the bridge, or dyke. (Lh, K.) Amr~ Ealayohi yadahu [ He passed his hand over him, or it ]. And Amr~ Elyh Alqalama [ He passed the pen over it, or across it ]. (A.) A^amorarotu Als~ik~iyna EalaY Haloqi Al$~aApi I passed the knife across the throat of the sheep, or goat. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., respecting the sound that is heard by the angels when a revelation is sent down, kaA_imoraAri AlHadiydi EalaY AlT~a$oti , meaning, Like the dragging, or drawing, (in a trans. sense,) of the iron over the copper basin: and in another trad., Sawota A_imoraAri Als~ilosilapi [ the sound of the dragging, or drawing, of the chain ]: or, accord. to the more common relation, Sawota miraAri Als~ilosilapi EalaY AlS~afaA , meaning, the sound of the dragging, (in an intrans. sense) and continuous running, of the chain upon the [ smooth ] rocks: (IAth, TA:) for ↓ maAr~a , inf. n. miraArN , signifies it (a thing) dragged, or became drawn along. (K, TA.) -A2- Amr~hu He twisted it tightly; namely, a rope, (S, A, Msb,) and a thread. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Ald~ahoru *uw naqoDK waA_imoraArK (tropical:) [ Time, or fortune , as it were, untwists and twists tightly ]. (A. TA.) [See art. nqD .] ― -b3- Hence also, Amr~hu (tropical:) He struggled, or strove, with him, (S, A,) and twisted about him, (S,) or twisted his neck, (A,) to throw him down; (S, A;) as also ↓ mAr~hu : (S:) or this latter signifies he twisted himself about him, and turned him round, to throw him down; (K,) [for yudiyruhu , in the K, we find in the L yuriyduhu , which latter is preferred by SM; but I prefer the former; for it also signifies] he turned him round, (namely, a camel,) in order to throw him down: (M:) or ↓ mAr~hN signifies he struggled, or strove, with him, and twisted his neck, (A,) to throw him down, (AHeyth, T, A,) (AHeyth, T, A,) the latter desiring to do the same; and the inf. n. is mumaAr~apN and miraArN : (AHeyth, T:) and ↓ A_imoraA^atuhu tumaAr~uhu his wife opposes him, and twists herself about him: (A, TA:) and ↓ miraAru AlHrobi is explained by As as signifying the striving to obtain the victory in war. (M.) -A3- Amr~ , (inf. n. You say, qado A^amar~a ha*aA AlT~aEaAmu fiY famiY This food has become bitter in my mouth: and in like manner you say of anything that becomes bitter. (TA.) You say also, A^amar~a Ealayohi AlEayo$u , and Ealayohi ↓ mar~a , (tropical:) [ Life became bitter to him ]. (A.) And Th cites, tumir~u EalayonaA AlA^aroDu mino A^ano naraY bihaA A^aniysFA wayaHolawoliY lanaA Albaladu Alqaforu [(tropical:) The land is displeasing to us from our seeing in it man, and the desolate country is pleasing to us ]: the poet makes tumir~u trans. by means of ElY , because it implies the meaning of taDiyqu [which is made trans. by means of the same particle]. (M, TA) You say also, A^amar~u waA^aHoluw , and A^amur~u waA^aHoluw , meaning (tropical:) I am bitter at one time, and I am sweet at one time. (IAar, M.) [See also 1 in art. Hlw .] ― -b2- But maA A^amar~a wamaA A^aHolaY signifies (tropical:) He said not. (IAar, S, M,) and he did not, (IAar, M,) a bitter thing, and he said not, (IAar, S, M,) and he did not, (IAar, M,) a sweet thing. (IAar, S, M.) You say, $atamaniY fulaAnN famaA A^amorarotu walaA A^aHolayotu (tropical:) Such a one reviled me, and I did not say a bitter thing, nor did I say a sweet thing. (Lh, T.) And fulaAnN maA yumir~u wamaA yuHoliY (tropical:) Such a one does not injure nor does he profit. (M, K. *) ― -b3- Amr~hu as syn. with mar~arahu : see 2.

sourceDefinition: : see 1, first signification, in three places. ― -b2- Also. It (a thing, M) went on in one [ uniform ] course or manner: (M, K:) it (an affair, A, or anything, Mgh) had a continuous course, or manner of being, &c.; (A, Mgh;) it continued in the same state; (Mgh:) it (a thing) continued, or obtained: (Msb:) it (said of blood) continued in a regular, uniform, or constant, course. (Mgh.) [And it is often said of a man.] -A2- [It also seems to signify It (a rope) became tightly twisted. ― -b2- And hence, (assumed tropical:) He, or it, became strong, or firm, like a rope tightly twisted: as in the following phrases.] Astmr~ biAl$~aYo'i (assumed tropical:) He became strong to bear the thing. (M, K. [See an ex. in a verse cited voce A^aSomaEu .]) Astmr~ mariyruhu (tropical:) He became firm; as also Astmr~t mariyratuhu : (A:) or his resolution, or determination, became firm, or strong; (S:) or he became strong, after being weak: and Astmr~t mariyratuhu his resistance ( $akiymap ) became firm. (TA.) You say also, Astmr~t mariyratuhu Ealayohi (tropical:) He became firm against him, or it: and his resistance ( $akiymap ) against him, or it, became strong: (K, TA:) and he became accustomed, or habituated, [or inured, ] to him, or it: a tropical signification, from the twisting of a rope. (TA.) ― -b3- [And hence, app.,] Astmr~ also signifies (assumed tropical:) His case, or state of affairs, became right, after having been bad or corrupt: (ISh, T, TA) he repented, and became good, righteous, or virtuous. (A [but not given as tropical].) -A3- As syn. with A^amar~a and mar~a , said of food, &c.: see 4.

sourceDefinition: Bitter; (S, A, Msb, K;) contr. of HulowN ; (K;) as also ↓ mariyrN and ↓ mumir~N : (A:) fem. mur~apN : (Msb, TA:) pl. masc. A^amoraArN , (T, S, M,) and pl. fem. maraAy^iru , contr. to rule, (Msb,) because mur~apN means xabiyvapu AlT~aEomi [ bad-tasted; and the pl. of xbyvp is xabaAy^ivu ]. (Msb, voce Hur~N .) You say baqolapN mur~apN [ A bitter leguminous plant ]: and ha*ihi Albaqolapu mino A^amoraAri Albuqowli [ This leguminous plant is one of the bitter leguminous plants ]. (T.) And $ajarapN mur~apN [ A bitter tree ]: pl. $ajarN maraAy^iru : the only instance of the kind except HaraAy^iru as pl. of Hur~apN . (Suh, in Msb, art. Hr .) ― -b2- [Hence the saying,] riEoYu bnY fulaAnK Almur~ataAni , (so in two copies of the S,) or ↓ Almur~ayaAni , (as in the K,) The pasturage of the sons of such a one is the [ bitter tree called ] A^alA=' and the [ bitter plant called ] $iyH . (S, K.) [For another application of Almur~ataAni , see A^amar~a .] ― -b3- Hence also, (TA,) Almur~u [ Myrrh; ] a certain medicine, (K,) like AlS~abir [or aloes ], (TA,) useful for cough, (K,) when sucked ( A_isotiHolaAbFA ) in the mouth, (TA,) and for the sting of the scorpion, (K,) when applied as a plaster, (TA,) and for worms of the intestines, (K,) when taken into the mouth in a dry state, or licked up from the palm of the hand: (TA:) also said to be the same as AlS~abiru : (TA:) pl. A^amoraArN . (K.) ― -b4- Ey$ mur~N (tropical:) [ A bitter life ]: like as one says [of the contr.], HulowN . (TA.) ― -b5- mar~ato Ealayohi A^amozaArN (tropical:) Afflictions or calamities [ came upon him ]. (TA.) ― -b6- nafosN mur~N (tropical:) A loathing mind, or stomach; syn. xabiyvapN kaArihapN . (TA.) ― -b7- A^abuw mur~apa A surname of Iblees, (S, K,) said to be from a daughter of his named mur~apu [ Bitter ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: A time; one time; [in the sense of the French fois; ] syn. taArapN : (Msb:) one action; a single action or act; (M, K;) as also ↓ mar~N : (M, K: [but see what follows:]) [ a bout; an instance; a case; and a single temporary offection or attack; a fit; as, for instance, of hunger, thirst, disease, and the like:] pl. mar~aAtN (A, Msb) and miraArN (S, M, A, Msb, K) and mirarN and ↓ mar~N [or rather this is a coll. gen. n. of which mar~apN is the n. un.] and muruwrN ; (M, K;) the last on the authority of Aboo-'Alee, and occurring in the following verse of Aboo-Dhu-eyb: tanak~arota baEodiY A^amo A^aSaAbaka HaAdivN mino Ald~ahori A^amo mar~ato Ealayoka muruwru [ Hast thou become altered since I saw thee, or hath an accident of fortune befallen thee, or have vicissitudes come upon thee? ] but Es-Sukkaree holds that mrwr is an inf. n.; and IJ says, I do not think this improbable, and that the verb is made fem. because the inf. n. implies muchness and genus. (M.) You say faEalotuhu mar~apF [ I did it once ], (A, Msb,) and mar~aAtK and miraArFA [ several times ]. (A.) [And biA@lomar~api At once. ] And laqiyahu *aAta mar~apK [ He met him once ]: only used adverbially: (M, K:) so says Sb. (M.) And laqiyahu *aAta AlmiraAri He met him many times: (M, K:) [or this has a different signification; for] you say fulaAnN yaSonaEu *`lika AlA^amora *aAta AlmiraAri meaning Such a one does that thing sometimes, and sometimes he leaves it undone. (ISk, S.) Also, jiy^otuhu mar~FA A^awo mar~ayoni , i. e., mar~apF A^awo mar~atayoni [ I came to him once or twice ]. (M, K.)
